key_actions.event: Declares himself caliph — break from Abbasid suzerainty.
Begins palace city Madinat al-Zahra outside Córdoba.
Grants Venice unprecedented trading privileges in exchange for naval help against Normans.
Defeats Pecheneg invasion at Levounion with Cuman aid.
Letter to Urban II requesting western mercenaries triggers the First Crusade.
Defeats Guthrum at Edington; Treaty of Wedmore creates Danelaw.
Recaptures London; styled 'King of the Anglo-Saxons'.
Commissions Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; translates Boethius and Augustine.

name: Abū al-Rayḥān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Bīrūnī
title: court_scholar

key_actions.summary: Completes Athār al-bāqiya (Vestiges of the Past), a comparative chronology of pre-Islamic Persian, Greek, Jewish, Christian, and Sabian calendars.

Completes Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (India), based on his accompanying Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns into northern India and learning Sanskrit. The work is the first sustained empirical study of Indian religion and astronomy by a non-Indian.
Completes Kitāb al-Qānūn al-Masʿūdī (The Canon Masudicus), the most extensive medieval Arabic astronomical compilation.
Begins his hadith-collection journeys at age sixteen, ultimately interviewing reported transmitters across Khurasan, Iraq, Hijaz, Syria, and Egypt over sixteen years.
Completes the Ṣaḥīḥ — ~7,275 hadith reports (with repetitions) selected from over 600,000 inspected by isnād criticism.
Dies at Khartank near Samarkand after expulsion from Nishapur by the local governor over a doctrinal dispute.
Appointed by vizier Nizam al-Mulk to the chair of Shafiʿi jurisprudence at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad.
Spiritual crisis. Abandons his Baghdad professorship for a decade of Sufi wandering across Damascus, Jerusalem, and Hijaz.
Returns to teaching at Nishapur; completes Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn (Revival of the Religious Sciences), reconciling Sunni orthodoxy with Sufi mysticism.
Defeats his brother al-Amin in the Fourth Fitna and accedes as caliph from Khurasan.
Imposes the Muʿtazila doctrine of the createdness of the Qurʾān as official caliphal theology; institutes the miḥna (inquisition) testing scholars on the doctrine.
Founds (or formalises) the Bayt al-Ḥikma ('House of Wisdom') at Baghdad, sponsoring the systematic translation of Greek mathematical, astronomical, and philosophical works into Arabic.

name: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakariyyāʾ al-Rāzī
title: court_physician

key_actions.summary: Becomes head of the Baghdad hospital under caliph al-Muktafi.
Completes Kitāb al-Manṣūrī (Liber Almansoris in Latin), a ten-volume medical encyclopedia.
Completes Kitāb al-Ḥāwī (The Comprehensive Book), the longest medical work of the Islamic Middle Ages — 23 surviving volumes of case-notes and references.

name: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī
title: scholar

key_actions.summary: Begins Jāmiʿ al-bayān ʿan taʾwīl āy al-Qurʾān, a verse-by-verse Qur'anic exegesis collecting earlier traditions.
Completes Taʾrīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk (History of the Prophets and Kings) — the most extensive Arabic universal history of the medieval period, from creation through 915 CE.
Dies at Baghdad. The Taʾrīkh becomes the single most-cited source for Umayyad and early Abbasid history.
Elected abbot of Bec in Normandy, succeeding his teacher Lanfranc.
Composes the Proslogion, containing the 'ontological argument' for the existence of God — the most famous single piece of medieval Latin philosophical reasoning.
Completes Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man) in exile in Italy, offering the satisfaction-theory of atonement that becomes standard Latin Christian soteriology.

key_actions.event: Overthrows Sonni Baru and takes power.
Hajj to Mecca; receives caliphal investiture as 'Caliph of Sudan'.
Codifies Songhai administration on Islamic-jurisprudence model.
Marries sister Anna to Vladimir of Kievan Rus' — Russian Christianization.
Defeats Bulgarian tsar Samuel at Kleidion; blinds 14,000 prisoners.
Final annexation of Bulgaria — Byzantine empire at maximum territorial extent.
Founds Monte Cassino monastery; writes the Rule of Benedict.
Begins 32-year Saxon Wars; forced conversion of Saxony to Christianity.
Defeats Lombards; takes title 'King of the Lombards'.
Crowned 'Emperor of the Romans' by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day.
Issues capitulary establishing missi dominici — itinerant royal inspectors.
Crowns son Louis as co-emperor; establishes dynastic succession.
Defeats Roman general Syagrius at Soissons — establishes Frankish authority in Gaul.
Baptism at Reims — first major Germanic king to convert to Nicene Christianity.
Defeats Visigoths at Vouillé; conquers Aquitaine.

key_actions.summary: Serves as one of the six priors of Florence (June–August 1300); aligns with the White Guelphs.
Condemned to exile in absentia by the Black Guelph faction; never returns to Florence.
Completes the Paradiso, the third canticle of the Divine Comedy, in his Ravenna exile shortly before his death (September 1321).
An Lushan rebellion breaks out; Du Fu spends the next four years separated from his family and unable to take up examination posts.
Settles in Chengdu at a thatched cottage where he composes a substantial portion of his surviving 1,500 poems.
Dies en route on the Yangtze. His poetic corpus is later collected by Tang and Song editors and elevated to canonical status by the 11th century.
Becomes regent for her ten-year-old son Constantine VI on the death of her husband Leo IV.
Convenes the Second Council of Nicaea, which restores the veneration of icons after sixty years of iconoclast imperial policy.
Deposes and blinds her son Constantine VI (15 August), reigning as sole emperor (basilissa) until her own deposition by the finance minister Nikephoros in 802.
Replaces Empress Wang as principal consort of Tang Gaozong; from then on dominates Tang governance.
Proclaims herself emperor — the only woman in Chinese imperial history to rule under her own dynastic name (the Zhou, 武周, 690–705).
Forced to abdicate in February 705 in a coup led by Tang loyalists; dies the same year. The Tang dynasty is formally restored.

key_actions.event: Converts to Christianity under tutelage of Frumentius.
Conquers Meroe; ends the Kingdom of Kush.

key_actions.summary: Begins composing the Shāhnāma ('Book of Kings'), drawing on the Sasanian-era Khvatāynāmag tradition and oral epic recensions.
Completes the Shāhnāma — ~60,000 couplets covering Iranian mythical, heroic, and historical eras down to the Arab conquest. Dedicates the work to Mahmud of Ghazni.
Dies at Tus. The Shāhnāma becomes the foundational text of New Persian as a literary language across the Persianate world, from Ottoman Anatolia to Mughal India.

key_actions.event: Receives papal approval for the Order of Friars Minor.
Receives stigmata on Mount La Verna.
Diet of Roncaglia — claims absolute imperial authority in northern Italy.
Italian League routs imperial army; Lombard cities effectively independent.
Treaty of Constance recognizes Lombard city-state autonomy.
Drowns in Saleph river en route to Third Crusade.
Proclaimed Genghis Khan at kurultai on Onon River.
Sacks Beijing — Jin dynasty driven southward.
Destroys Khwarezmian Empire; sacks Samarkand and Merv.

key_actions.summary: Appointed Comptroller of Customs at the Port of London by Edward III, securing a stable income through the next twelve years.
Begins composing Troilus and Criseyde (~8,000 lines), drawn primarily from Boccaccio's Il Filostrato.
Begins the Canterbury Tales, a frame-narrative cycle that remains unfinished at his death in October 1400.

key_actions.event: Leads First Crusade siege and capture of Jerusalem.
Refuses crown of Jerusalem; takes title 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.

provenance.attestation: his work History of the Franks referenced as source for Frankish maps 511-561

key_actions.summary: Becomes a hafiz (memoriser of the Qur'an), the etymology of his takhalluṣ (pen-name).
Patronised at the Muzaffarid court at Shiraz; composes ghazals widely circulated across the Persianate world during his lifetime.
Dies at Shiraz. His Dīwān — ~500 ghazals collected after his death — becomes the canonical text of Persian lyric poetry.

key_actions.event: Exchanges embassies with Charlemagne; gifts include a white elephant.
Founds Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad.
Sacks Heraclea; forces Byzantine tribute.

name: Henry III of England (Lord of Ireland)

key_actions.summary: Sails from Carthage with the Carthaginian-African fleet; deposes the tyrant Phocas at Constantinople.
Defeats the Sasanian Persian army at the Battle of Nineveh (12 December), inflicting the decisive defeat of a generation-long Roman-Persian war.
Roman armies under Vahan are destroyed by the early Caliphate at the Battle of the Yarmuk (August 636), opening Syria, Palestine, and Egypt to Arab conquest.
Reports the visionary experience that initiates the composition of Scivias; her abbot Volmar and Pope Eugenius III endorse the writings at the synod of Trier (1147–48).
Completes Scivias (Know the Ways), a trilogy of 26 visions with extensive illuminations.
Begins her four preaching tours through the Rhineland; an extraordinary public role for a 12th-century woman.
Despatched west from the Mongol heartland by his brother Möngke with orders to subjugate Iran, Iraq, and Syria.
Destroys the Nizari Ismaili strongholds in northern Iran, including Alamut on 15 December 1256.
Sacks Baghdad (29 January – 10 February 1258) and executes the Abbasid caliph al-Mustaʿṣim, ending the Abbasid caliphate as a political institution.
Completes the Muqaddimah, the prolegomenon to his universal history, while in retreat at the castle of Qalʿat ibn Salāma (near Frenda, modern Algeria).
Settles in Cairo under Mamluk patronage; appointed grand qadi of the Maliki school (1384, again 1399, 1401, 1402, 1404).
Negotiates with Timur outside besieged Damascus; converses with the conqueror on universal-historical themes.

name_variants: Abū Zayd ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Khaldūn al-Ḥaḍramī

key_actions.summary: Appointed qadi of Seville, then chief qadi of Cordoba in 1182, by Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf.
Completes Tahāfut al-tahāfut (Incoherence of the Incoherence), defending Aristotelian rationalism against al-Ghazali.
Briefly exiled by caliph al-Mansur under pressure from Maliki jurists; pardoned before his death in Marrakesh (1198).

name_variants: Abū al-Walīd Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Rushd

key_actions.summary: Begins composing Kitāb al-Shifāʾ (The Book of Healing), a multi-volume philosophical encyclopedia.
Completes Al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb (The Canon of Medicine), the standard medical textbook of the Islamic world and (via Latin translation) of medieval European universities until the 17th century.
Dies at Hamadan; leaves a Peripatetic philosophical tradition (mashshāʾī) that decisively shapes both Sunni theology and Latin scholasticism via Albertus Magnus and Aquinas.

name_variants: Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd Allāh Ibn Sīnā

key_actions.event: Proclaimed chakravartin (universal monarch) at Mount Mahendraparvata — foundation of Khmer Empire.
Begins compilation of Corpus Juris Civilis under Tribonian.
Quells Nika Riots; rebuilds Constantinople, including Hagia Sophia.
Belisarius reconquers North Africa from Vandals.
Belisarius takes Ravenna from Ostrogoths; Italian reconquest underway.
Plague of Justinian devastates the empire — halts further expansion.
Proclaims Yuan Dynasty — Mongol rule of China.
Defeats last Southern Song forces at Yamen; reunifies China.
Second Mongol invasion of Japan defeated by typhoon (kamikaze).
Issues Ordinatio Imperii dividing inheritance among sons — embeds future fragmentation.
Deposed at Field of Lies; reinstated 834.

key_actions.summary: Maimonides's family flees Cordoba after the Almohad conquest forces conversion or exile on the Andalusi Jewish community.
Completes Mishneh Torah, a 14-volume systematic codification of rabbinic law in Hebrew.
Completes Dalālat al-Ḥāʾirīn (Guide for the Perplexed) in Judeo-Arabic in Cairo, reconciling Aristotelian philosophy with rabbinic Judaism.

key_actions.event: Hajj to Mecca with caravan that destabilises Egyptian gold market for a decade.
Returns with Andalusi architect al-Sahili — builds Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu.
Reports first revelations in Hira cave outside Mecca.
Hijra — migration to Medina; year 1 of Islamic calendar.
Conquers Mecca; cleanses Kaaba of idols.
Delivers Farewell Sermon; dies at Medina.

key_actions.summary: Founds the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad, the first major endowed Islamic college and template for the wider madrasa system.
Completes the Siyāsatnāma (Book of Government), a mirror-for-princes treatise written for Sultan Malik-Shah I.
Assassinated in October 1092 near Nahavand, almost certainly by Nizari Ismaili agents acting on Hasan-i Sabbah's orders.

name_variants: Abu Ali Hasan ibn Ali Tusi

key_actions.summary: Completes Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra, advancing the geometric solution of cubic equations.
Co-leads the Seljuk astronomical reform under Malik-Shah that produces the Jalali calendar — more accurate over a millennium than the later Gregorian.
Dies at Nishapur. His Rubāʿīyāt — four-line quatrains on themes of mortality, doubt, and pleasure — survive in fragmentary recensions, made famous in Europe by Edward FitzGerald's 1859 paraphrase.

name_variants: Ghiyāth al-Dīn Abū al-Fatḥ ʿUmar ibn Ibrāhīm Nīshābūrī

key_actions.event: Defeats Magyar invasion at Lechfeld — ends 60 years of raids.
Crowned emperor by John XII in Rome — re-foundation of Western imperial title.

key_actions.summary: Climbs Mont Ventoux with his brother Gherardo (26 April), an event he later treats in De vita solitaria as a turn toward inner-directed contemplation.
Crowned poet laureate on the Capitoline Hill at Rome (8 April), the first such laureation since antiquity — a deliberate revival of classical practice.
Discovers Cicero's letters to Atticus at the Verona Chapter Library; the find decisively shapes the humanist epistolary mode he subsequently develops.

key_actions.event: Conquers Cyprus en route to Third Crusade; sells it to Templars.
Takes Acre after two-year Crusader siege.
Negotiates Treaty of Jaffa with Saladin.
Released from Habsburg captivity for ransom of 150,000 marks.

key_actions.summary: Joins the Franciscans; subsequently writes in conditions of restricted output, possibly under direct supervision.
Sends Opus Majus, Opus Minus, and Opus Tertium to Clement IV; the trilogy argues for experimental method, mathematical natural philosophy, and improved calendar science.
Reportedly imprisoned by the Franciscan general Jerome of Ascoli (later Pope Nicholas IV) for 'suspected novelties'; released around 1290.
Encounters the wandering dervish Shams al-Dīn Tabrīzī at Konya; their three-year companionship transforms Rumi from a conventional jurist into a poet of ecstatic mysticism.
Begins composing the Mathnawī-i Maʿnawī, a six-book, ~25,000-couplet didactic poem in Persian — the central work of Persian Sufi literature.
Dies at Konya. His son Sultan Walad institutionalises the Sufi community around him as the Mevlevī order, with its characteristic samā (whirling) ceremony.

key_actions.event: Abolishes Fatimid Caliphate; rules Egypt for Abbasids nominally.
Defeats Crusader army at Hattin; captures the True Cross.
Recaptures Jerusalem after 88 years of Christian rule.
Treaty of Jaffa with Richard the Lionheart concludes Third Crusade.
Begins conquest campaigns recorded in Allahabad pillar inscription.
Subdues 21 kings of northern India; vassalizes Vakataka, Pallavas.
Xuanwu Gate incident; kills brothers and forces father's abdication.
Defeats Eastern Turkic Khaganate; takes title 'Tian Kehan' (heavenly khagan).
Sends Princess Wencheng to marry Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo.
Codifies Tang Code — foundation of East Asian legal traditions.

key_actions.summary: Marries the future emperor Justinian, after the lex restoring senatorial-grade marriage rights to former actresses (the Lex de nuptiis) is enacted by Justin I.
Reportedly speaks against fleeing the capital during the Nika riots — 'purple is the noblest shroud' — stiffening Justinian's resolve and securing the dynasty.

Dies of cancer in June 548. Justinian, surviving her by 17 years, never remarries; her domestic policy initiatives (including legislation against forced prostitution) are continued in his later Novellae.

key_actions.event: Begins Summa Theologiae at Rome.
Dies en route to Council of Lyon.

key_actions.summary: Takes Balkh and is proclaimed Emir at Samarkand, claiming legitimacy through marriage to a Chinggisid princess (the source of his title gurkan, 'son-in-law').
Sacks Delhi after defeating the Tughluq sultan Mahmud II at the Battle of Delhi.
Defeats the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara (28 July), capturing Bayezid himself and arresting Ottoman expansion for half a century.

key_actions.event: Battle of Yarmouk — defeats Byzantine field army; Levant lost to Islam.
Conquers Jerusalem; visits in person, refuses to pray in Holy Sepulchre.
Battle of Nahavand ends Sasanian resistance; Persia conquered.
Mass baptism of Kiev — Orthodox Christianization of Rus'.
Marries Anna Porphyrogenita, Basil II's sister.
Defeats Harold Godwinson at Hastings; crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day.
Commissions Domesday Book — most detailed pre-modern land survey in Europe.
Becomes empress dowager after Gaozong's death; effectively rules.
Founds her own Zhou dynasty; only woman to formally rule China as emperor.
Forced to abdicate; Tang restored.
